newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition finalises tax reform framework.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition finalises tax reform framework.

text.p: Germany's coalition government overcame differences on Wednesday to agree the framework of tax reforms designed to boost job creation and help Chancellor Helmut Kohl win election for a record fifth time next year.
After marathon talks, a tax working commission chaired by Finance Minister Theo Waigel agreed a package featuring big income tax cuts that will take effect in 1999.
"This is the biggest tax reform in the history of the German Federal Republic," Waigel told reporters after all-day talks which stretched into the evening.
The plan should win the blessing of the three parties in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling alliance on Thursday before being unveiled by Waigel later in the day (1700 GMT).

Waigel told reporters that the reform would cut 70 billion marks ($43 billion) in taxes. Taking into account the scrapping of tax breaks and a possible compensating rise in indirect taxes, Germans will pay 30 billion marks less in taxes at the end of the day.

After a tense few days, Waigel struck a compromise deal on income taxes which met his wish to maintain Germany's unusual linear system, while accepting demands from junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) for a low starting rate.
The new model will look like this: Single earners will pay no tax on the first 13,000 marks they earn. A bottom rate of 15 percent will kick in on income from 13,000 to 20,000 marks.

Earnings above that level will be taxed on a sliding scale starting at 22 percent and rising to 39 percent at 90,000 marks -- with the peak threshold higher than earlier indicated by commission sources.
The tax model would slash Germany's existing rates, which start at 26 percent and rise to a peak of 53 percent.
Under the reform, corporation tax will also fall to 35 percent from 47 percent in 1998.
Offsetting the reductions will be the scrapping of a slew of tax exemptions which make Germany's tax system one of the most opaque -- and abuse-prone -- in the world.

Hermann Otto Solms, chief FDP tax negotiator, said he was satisfied with the result. "We have put together a good plan," he told reporters, adding it would boost both the coalition government and the hopes of Germany's four million jobless.

A decision on the most controversial issue in the reform -- whether to raise Germany's 15 percent rate of value-added tax to help pay for cuts in direct taxes -- was postponed and will not be decided on by the coalition parties on Thursday.

Waigel favours a one-percentage point increase in VAT, but has run into crossfire from up-and-coming regional leaders in Kohl's Christian Democrat party (CDU) who have said he should resign if he raises indirect taxes.

A majority in the CDU leadership, however, wants a bigger VAT rise to help bail out Germany's cash-strapped social security system which is struggling to cope with unemployment set to break post-war records this winter.
Waigel did not comment directly on the VAT issue, saying that there was "a certain outstanding amount" in the tax reform which would need to be covered on the revenue side.

He added that the commission had also agreed on a model on taxing pensions under which people receiving average retirement benefits would pay no taxes. Taxation of other welfare benefits will also be rejigged, but the state would end up spending more than it receives, Waigel said. ($1=1.6415 Mark)
